entities.name: Johann Kaspar Mörikofer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johann Kaspar Mörikofer (1799–1877) was a pioneering Swiss literary and ecclesiastical historian, whose meticulous scholarship significantly shaped the understanding of both Swiss national literature and the Protestant Reformation within its borders. Born in Frauenfeld on October 11, 1799, and dying in Bern on October 17, 1877, Mörikofer dedicated his life to archival research and comprehensive synthesis, establishing foundational narratives for the 18th-century Swiss literary landscape and, most notably, providing the definitive 19th-century biography of Huldrych Zwingli, a key figure in the European Reformation.

Mörikofer's major contributions include his two-volume *Die schweizerische Litteratur des achtzehnten Jahrhunderts* (1861–1862), which systematically cataloged and analyzed the literary output of the Swiss Enlightenment, and his monumental *Ulrich Zwingli: Nach den urkundlichen Quellen* (1867–1869). This three-volume biography of Zwingli, meticulously drawing from primary sources, became the standard work on the Reformer for decades, offering a nuanced portrait that corrected earlier interpretations and solidified Zwingli's intellectual and theological contributions. His work on Protestant refugees in Switzerland further illuminated the nation's historical role as a haven during religious upheavals.

Mörikofer's legacy rests on his role in professionalizing Swiss historical scholarship, particularly in literary and ecclesiastical domains. His commitment to primary source research and comprehensive narrative construction influenced subsequent generations of Swiss historians, providing a robust methodological framework for studying national identity through its cultural and religious past. His Zwingli biography, in particular, remained a crucial reference point for theologians and historians well into the 20th century, fostering a deeper appreciation for the distinct character of the Swiss Reformation compared to its German and Genevan counterparts.
